Nice to meet you too, Doc. Well, I’m here because... honestly, it’s getting to the point where I keep forgetting things I really, really shouldn’t. And I don’t mean just walking into a room and forgetting why—everybody my age does that, right? I mean important stuff. Like my heart follow-up appointments. I had this issue a bit ago, and the cardiologist wanted to check in on me, you know, just to be safe and make sure everything is ticking right. Well, the day of the appointment comes and goes, completely flew right out of my head. Didn't even register. And then when they leave a voicemail about it, I tell myself, "Okay, call them back right now," but then the doorbell rings, or I decide I need to go check the mail, and boom—I completely forget to call the clinic back. It took me weeks just to get it sorted out! It’s driving me up the wall. 

And it’s not just medical stuff, it’s my day-to-day. Since I stopped working, I try to keep busy, do a little handyman work, fix things around the house, that sort of thing. But I’ll get all geared up for a repair job, walk all the way out to the shed or over to the side of the house, and realize I showed up without the right tools. I’ll be standing there looking at a loose board and realize I brought a wrench instead of a hammer, or I just brought nothing at all because I got distracted on the walk over. I have to make five trips back and forth to the garage just to do one simple job. I just... I don't know, my brain just won't hold onto what I'm supposed to be doing, and it's exhausting.
Have these forgetfulness problems gotten worse compared with how you used to be?

Well, that’s the thing, Doc. That’s exactly the thing. Have they gotten worse? I mean, yes and no? Mostly no, I think. But let me explain, because it’s not a simple yes or no. 

See, back when I was working—I was a foreman, you know, constantly moving, constantly putting out fires, dealing with this guy, dealing with that guy. My brain was always going a mile a minute, but it worked for me then. If I forgot to grab a tool, well, I was already practically running across the site to check on something else anyway, so it didn't seem like a big deal. I was always on the go, always talking to somebody, always jumping from one problem to the next. People just thought, "Oh, that’s just how he is, he’s a high-energy guy." And I was! I still am! I can't sit still for the life of me. 

But now? Now that I’m retired and just puttering around the house? It’s like all that energy doesn’t have anywhere productive to go, so the forgetfulness just... stands out more, you know? Like with the tools. I never used to just do one repair job at a time. I’d be doing three things at once. But now, I tell myself, "Okay, today I am fixing the porch railing." And then I go out there without the hammer, and my wife looks at me like I’m losing my marbles. 

So, I don’t think my brain is actually worse at remembering things than it was thirty years ago. I think I’ve always been this way—always a bit scattered, always a bit impulsive, always forgetting the little details because I’m already thinking about the next five things I want to do. It’s just that now, without the chaos of the job site to hide it, it’s a lot more obvious when I mess up. Like the cardiologist appointment. If I was working, my secretary would have reminded me, or I would have had it written on the big whiteboard in the office. Now, it’s just me and a sticky note that I probably threw away because I needed to use the pen to write down a grocery list, which I also forgot at home. So, worse? Probably not. More annoying? Absolutely. It's just... it's like a motor that won't shut off, but the car is in park. Does that make sense?
When you think back to grade school, were you already the kind of kid who was distractible or had trouble staying organized?

Oh boy, grade school. If my mother were still around, she would have an absolute earful for you about that. I grew up in a time when they didn't really have a way to describe kids like me, you know? You were just considered a handful, or a troublemaker, or maybe just a boy with way too much pep. I’d be up sharpening my pencil, or leaning over to look out the window, or just standing up for no reason at all.
